situation: A presidential campaign's sign-up page shows one big image or video above a single button. Staff strongly favour an inspiring campaign video. Millions of people will see the page.
goal: Get the largest share of visitors to sign up.
options: The campaign video, with a 'Sign Up' button
A family photo, with a 'Learn More' button
The campaign video, with a 'Learn More' button
outcome: In a test of 4 buttons x 6 media, 'Learn More' with the family image won: an 11.6% sign-up rate versus 8.26% for the original, a 40.6% improvement. Every video did worse than every image.

situation: 1747. Twelve sailors on a navy ship have scurvy. You can give each pair of patients one of several proposed remedies for a few days.
goal: Find out which remedy actually cures scurvy.
options: Cider
Elixir of vitriol (dilute sulfuric acid)
Vinegar
Seawater
Two oranges and a lemon
A spicy paste with barley water
outcome: James Lind ran this comparison in 1747. The pair given oranges and a lemon recovered; it was an early controlled trial of competing remedies.

situation: Nigeria, 1966. Smallpox outbreaks are flaring up, and there is far too little vaccine to vaccinate everyone. The standard approach at the time is mass vaccination.
goal: Stop the outbreaks with the vaccine available.
options: Vaccinate as many people as possible, wherever teams can reach
Find cases fast and vaccinate the people exposed to them
Reserve the vaccine for the biggest cities
outcome: William Foege's surveillance and ring-vaccination strategy targeted people exposed to cases, so limited vaccine sufficed to stop outbreaks. The approach became key to global eradication.

situation: Parents at several day-care centres keep picking their children up late, so staff have to stay on.
options: Introduce a small fine for each late pickup
Don't fine; keep relying on parents' sense of obligation
Try the fine, and remove it if lateness doesn't fall
outcome: In Israeli day-care centres a fine for lateness increased late pickups: parents treated it as a price. When the fine was removed, lateness stayed at the higher level (Gneezy & Rustichini, 'A Fine is a Price', 2000).

situation: A company runs free on-site flu-shot clinics and mails every employee a reminder with the clinic times.
goal: Raise the share of employees who get vaccinated.
options: The standard reminder mailer
The mailer plus a blank to write down the date you plan to go
The mailer plus a blank to write down the date and the time you plan to go
outcome: Against a 33.1% control rate, the date-only prompt raised vaccination 1.5 percentage points (not statistically significant); the date-and-time prompt raised it 4.2 points (significant).

situation: A company's retirement plan has generous matching, but many new hires never enrol.
options: Keep enrolment opt-in and send clearer reminders
Enrol new hires automatically and let them opt out
outcome: When the company switched to automatic enrolment, with no change to the plan's economics, savings behaviour 'dramatically changed' (Madrian & Shea). A side effect: many people stayed at the low default rate.

situation: A country's organ-donor register has few sign-ups, though most people say they support donation.
goal: Raise the share of people who are donors.
options: Keep opt-in registration and run awareness campaigns
Make everyone a donor by default, with an easy opt-out
outcome: Across European countries, those with opt-out (presumed consent) defaults had far higher effective consent rates than opt-in countries (Johnson & Goldstein, 'Do Defaults Save Lives?', 2003). This is a comparison between countries, not a randomized trial.

situation: A city wants to charge drivers to enter its centre to cut congestion. Many residents oppose it, and nobody knows how traffic will respond.
goal: Get a lasting traffic reduction that the public accepts.
options: Introduce it permanently now
Run it as a time-limited trial, then put it to a referendum
Shelve the idea until opinion shifts
outcome: Stockholm ran a seven-month trial in 2006 and held a referendum afterwards. Stockholm municipality voted yes, and the charge became permanent on 1 August 2007.

situation: 1978. A structural engineer finds that his own new skyscraper could collapse in a strong storm: the welded joints he designed were switched to bolted ones during construction, and diagonal winds were never checked.
options: Keep quiet; a storm that strong is unlikely
Tell the owners and officials, and reinforce the joints
Quietly check the numbers again next year
outcome: William LeMessurier disclosed the problem. From August 1978 crews welded steel panels over the bolted joints at night, finishing that October.

situation: World War II. Bombers return from missions with bullet holes clustered in some areas and few in others. Armour is heavy, so only part of each plane can be protected.
options: Armour the areas with the most holes on returning planes
Armour the areas where returning planes show few or no holes
Spread thin armour evenly over the whole plane
outcome: Abraham Wald's analysis treated the returning planes as survivors: hits in the areas that show few holes are the ones that bring planes down. Reinforcing only where survivors were hit would miss the point.

situation: 1847, Vienna. In one of a hospital's two maternity clinics, run by doctors who also perform autopsies, mothers die of childbed fever far more often than in the clinic run by midwives.
goal: Cut maternal deaths in the doctors' clinic.
options: Improve ventilation in the doctors' clinic
Have doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime solution before examining patients
Move more births to the midwives' clinic
outcome: Semmelweis introduced hand-washing with chlorinated lime, and maternal mortality dropped from 18% to under 2%. Many doctors rejected his findings at the time.

situation: ICU patients keep getting bloodstream infections from central lines, though the prevention steps are well known.
goal: Cut central-line infections across a state's ICUs.
options: More lectures on infection control
A short checklist of the key steps, used for every line
Switch to more expensive catheters
outcome: Peter Pronovost's ICU checklist protocol was credited with saving about 1,500 lives and $100 million in Michigan over 18 months.

situation: A carmaker's early models were unreliable, and its sales collapsed with its reputation. Its newer cars are much better, but buyers don't believe it.
options: Cut prices further
Offer a 10-year / 100,000-mile powertrain warranty
Run an ad campaign about the improved quality
outcome: Hyundai added a 10-year / 100,000-mile powertrain warranty in the US. By 2004 sales had increased dramatically and its reputation had improved.

situation: 1982. Someone has poisoned bottles of a leading painkiller on store shelves, and several people have died. The tampering seems to be local.
goal: Protect the public and the brand.
options: Recall only the affected batch
Recall the product nationwide
Say nothing until the police finish investigating
outcome: Johnson & Johnson issued a nationwide recall of an estimated 31 million bottles. Tylenol's market share fell from 35% to 8% but rebounded within a year, which is credited to the prompt reaction.

situation: An inventor's bagless vacuum outperforms everything on the market, but UK manufacturers and distributors refuse it because it would kill their dust-bag sales.
options: Keep pitching UK manufacturers
Launch it abroad through a channel that doesn't depend on them
Sell the patent and move on
outcome: Dyson launched the vacuum in Japan through catalogue sales, and later made it under his own name.
